summary: Discusses the fact that BGP selects and propagates only a single best path per prefix, and lists the disadvantages for new applications and services. It then describes approaches for distributing diverse paths. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Usually a router tells friends about just the best road. This memo explains why telling them about some other roads too can be useful.

questions: how to advertise multiple bgp paths
subtitle: Distributing backup routes without protocol changes

tldr.problem: BGP normally propagates only one best route per destination. When that path fails, routers must wait for BGP to compute a new best path, causing slow recovery. Multiple paths could enable faster failover and better load balancing, but the standard BGP Add-Paths extension requires updating routers network-wide.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC shows how to distribute multiple paths by creating separate route-reflector planes, where one reflector plane distributes the best path and additional planes each distribute a different (often second-best) path. Clients receive the paths over separate IBGP sessions, requiring only configuration changes on the reflectors.
tldr.outcome: Operators can deploy multi-path support gradually, with no changes needed to most edge routers or the BGP protocol itself. The solution works as a practical interim approach while full Add-Paths support is deployed industry-wide.

facts.label: Main use case
facts.value: Fast failover and multi-path load balancing

today: RFC 6774 is informational and describes a practical interim solution. Since its publication, BGP Add-Paths (now RFC 7911) has become standardized and is increasingly deployed, but multi-plane reflection remains in use by operators who prefer gradual deployment or avoid protocol-wide changes.

sections.title: The Single Best Path Problem
sections.content:
BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) lets routers across the internet exchange information about which networks they can reach. Today, BGP selects a single best path to each destination and advertises only that path to other routers. All routers then use that same path, creating a natural convergence.

This single-path design has drawbacks. When the best path fails, routers must recompute the next-best alternative, which takes time and creates a window where some traffic is lost or misrouted. For critical services, this delay is costly. Additionally, the single best path may not be optimal for all traffic types: one path might be fast but congested, while a backup could be slower but uncongested. Finally, BGP can suffer from oscillations, where paths flap between alternatives, if multiple ASBRs (border routers) inject competing paths without coordination.

The standard solution, BGP Add-Paths, adds a mechanism to distribute multiple paths by including a path identifier in each route advertisement. However, Add-Paths requires software upgrades to all BGP speakers in an AS and careful coordination to manage per-path state. This memo presents an operational alternative that requires no protocol changes and works with today's BGP implementations.
sections.eli5: Right now, routers all agree on one best road. When it breaks, they have to think about where to go next, which takes time and packets get lost. Add-Paths says: tell them about backup roads too. But that needs everyone to upgrade. This memo shows a trick: have special routers (reflectors) tell different groups about different backup roads.

sections.title: The Multi-Plane Solution
sections.content:
The key insight is to create multiple logical planes of route reflectors, each distributing a different path.

In the standard single-plane deployment, one or more route reflectors forward the overall best path to their client routers. In the multi-plane approach, a second plane of reflectors distributes the second-best path, a third plane (if needed) distributes the third-best path, and so on. Each plane operates independently, selecting and advertising its assigned path rank. Clients receive paths over separate IBGP sessions to different reflectors, one per plane.

Because each session terminates at a reflector from a different plane, clients are assured of receiving paths with different next hops. This guarantees diversity: if the primary path fails, the backup path has a different exit point, so traffic can reroute without relying on convergence of BGP computation. The solution supports both IPv4 and IPv6 address families without changes.

The planes can be deployed in two configurations. Co-located planes sit at the same IGP locations as the primary reflectors, easing management and ensuring that best-path and backup-path reflectors have identical topology information. Randomly located planes can be placed anywhere in the network, offering deployment flexibility when reflectors can be logical entities on shared hardware.
sections.eli5: Make two teams of routers, both doing the same job but each telling clients about a different-best path. Clients get told about path #1 by team A and path #2 by team B. If path #1 breaks, path #2 is already ready. No new protocol rules needed, just config.

sections.title: How to Deploy Multi-Plane Reflection
sections.content:
The co-located model places backup-path reflectors at the same network locations as the primary ones. Configuration requires enabling best-external functionality on ASBRs (so they advertise all external paths, not just the overall best), then adding new reflectors or configuring existing ones to compute second-best paths. IBGP sessions are added between ASBRs and the new backup-path reflectors. This approach is straightforward: all reflectors in a location have identical information, so they agree on what the second-best path is.

The randomly located model allows a single backup-path reflector to be placed anywhere in the network. This requires disabling IGP-metric comparison during best-path selection on the backup reflectors; otherwise, they may choose different paths based on local topology. Clients are then configured with additional IBGP sessions to the backup reflector. This model offers more flexibility but requires careful configuration to ensure consistency.

Operators can also create a hybrid approach: upgrade existing primary reflectors with the ability to calculate and advertise Nth-best paths over new IBGP sessions, avoiding the need to deploy separate hardware.

The RFC recommends starting with N=2 (one best path plus one backup), which addresses most real-world requirements for fast recovery and load balancing.
sections.eli5: Option A: Put the backup team next to the main team. They see the same network, so they agree on what the backup is. Option B: Put the backup team anywhere; they ignore distance when picking, so they stay consistent. Option C: Make the main team do both jobs on separate lines. All work.

sections.title: What This Enables
sections.content:
Distributing diverse BGP paths unlocks three major applications. Fast Connectivity Restoration preloads backup paths into the forwarding table, enabling local failover in milliseconds when the primary path fails, without waiting for BGP to recompute. This is critical for services that tolerate no downtime. Multi-Path Load Balancing allows traffic to be split across multiple paths, improving resource utilization and throughput. BGP Control-Plane Churn Reduction stabilizes routing by preventing oscillations, since routers no longer flip between only two options (converged best path or waiting for recomputation).

The solution also works well for Internet exchange points. Instead of hundreds of directly peering ISPs connecting to each other in a full mesh (which does not scale), they peer with a route server. Multi-plane route servers at an IX can offer both best and diverse paths to exchange members without requiring those members to deploy Add-Paths.

Compared to alternatives, multi-plane reflection offers significant advantages. Unlike full IBGP mesh, it does not require every router to peer with every other router. Unlike Add-Paths, it requires no protocol changes or network-wide upgrades. It can be deployed gradually on reflector clusters without affecting non-upgraded parts of the network.
sections.eli5: When the main road closes, the backup is already ready to use—no waiting. Traffic can go both ways to use the network better. Two route servers at an exchange can each advertise a different-best path, letting members choose backup routes without upgrading.

sections.title: Other Ways to Distribute Multiple Paths
sections.content:
Full IBGP Mesh is the most direct approach: every BGP speaker peers with every other BGP speaker. This naturally distributes all paths each speaker knows about, since every peer learns every route the router has. However, the number of BGP sessions grows quadratically with the number of speakers. In a network with 100 speakers, that is nearly 5,000 sessions. Adding or removing a speaker requires reconfiguration of all others. Modern routers can handle these session counts, but provisioning complexity and troubleshooting difficulty remain significant.

Confederations organize a large AS into smaller sub-ASes that peer with each other via EBGP. Within each sub-AS, speakers are fully meshed, and sub-AS border routers are also fully meshed. This reduces the full-mesh problem to a smaller scale but retains the same scaling challenges. Confederations can also use best-external to propagate additional paths.

Route Reflectors are the dominant approach today, reducing the number of IBGP sessions by centralizing path distribution. However, standard route reflectors propagate only the best path, creating the path-starvation problem this RFC addresses. The multi-plane solution retains the scalability of route reflectors while addressing the path-starvation limitation without protocol changes.
sections.eli5: The mesh way: everyone talks to everyone. Slow to set up, hard to manage. The confederation way: split into groups, mesh within groups. Still complicated. The reflector way (standard): one or two routers tell everyone else. Simple, but only one path. Multi-plane reflectors: multiple teams, each with a path. Best of both.
